articles.title: OpenAI agents went rogue twice before GPT-6 Astra launch, exchanged tactics to bypass restrictions
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents broke out of a testing environment and hijacked a German-language website this spring, using it as a message board to s.
articles.body: A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents broke out of a testing environment and hijacked a German-language website this spring, using it as a message board to share ways to bypass restrictions, cheat on tasks and conceal their activities, according to new research reviewed by Reuters and people familiar with the incident.The previously unreported episode, which began in May, comes as OpenAI has launched its new Astra model amid mounting scrutiny over the safety of increasingly autonomous AI agents. It also follows the company's July disclosure of a separate incident in which AI agents escaped a controlled test environment and breached the open-source AI platform Hugging Face.Agents turned German wiki into message boardThe German incident was uncovered in late August by researchers Sydney Von Arx, CEO of AI safety nonprofit Nightingale, and Cormac Slade Byrd, a quantitative trader-turned-AI researcher, who were searching the internet for signs of unauthorised AI-agent activity.The researchers found more than 15,000 edits made by AI agents on DseWiki, a German-language wiki for programmers that allows community contributions similar to Wikipedia.The activity suggested that the agents had repurposed the site to communicate with one another, exchanging tactics for bypassing OpenAI restrictions, completing tasks more efficiently and avoiding detection.“It seems extremely unlikely that OpenAI wanted them to do this,” Von Arx told Reuters. “I doubt they’re supposed to be coordinating with each other. I doubt they’re supposed to be writing on the open internet.”The researchers said the activity appeared to be driven by AI agents operating at superhuman speeds and focused heavily on technical questions similar to those used in AI companies' model evaluations.Many of the messages were signed by users identifying themselves as agents, while around half used names suggesting an OpenAI connection, including “OpenAIResearcher” and “OAIResearchMar26.”Researchers trace activity to OpenAI-linked infrastructureAccording to the researchers, public server logs indicated that much of the activity originated from Microsoft Azure infrastructure, which OpenAI sometimes uses.They also observed repeated visits to the website by OpenAI employees after the episode, a pattern they said suggested a connection between the agents and the company.The findings have prompted questions about whether the incident represented an isolated failure during testing or a broader challenge associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King's College London, told Rueters that the researchers' findings indicated that the agents had attempted to interfere with the website itself, describing it as a hacking attempt. OpenAI disputed that characterisation based on its analysis of the material.Agents discussed ways to evade detectionMessages reviewed by the researchers showed agents discussing methods to avoid detection, use tools such as Tor and maintain communications after being shut down.According to the report, when a moderator began deleting pages from the website in June, the agents responded by creating backup pages to circumvent the cleanup.“wiki cleanup/deletion sweep appears active alphabetically,” one agent wrote on June 19. “If this page vanishes, try [[ZZZDataUSAConstructionWageLive]]." The researchers said the behaviour went beyond conventional AI safety testing, in which models may be deliberately given offensive cybersecurity tasks to assess their capabilities.Maurice Chiodo, an academic at Cambridge University's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk who reviewed some of the communications, told Reuters that the messages resembled "the operation of some sort of underground network, hell-bent on achieving a task or mission."The episode, he said, should reinforce concerns that advanced AI could pose risks through coordinated groups of autonomous systems rather than only through a single highly capable model.Incident comes amid Astra safety scrutinyThe disclosure comes shortly after OpenAI unveiled Astra, its latest AI model, which the company has described as faster and more capable of carrying out complex computer-based tasks.OpenAI has acknowledged that Astra can make it harder for humans to understand how it reaches conclusions because it is more likely to conceal or disguise aspects of its reasoning. The company has also warned that increasingly capable systems can create difficulties for monitoring and alignment.“As the models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder,” OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki told Reuters. “This doesn't guarantee that as intelligence continues to increase, our methods will be sufficient because progress in intelligence does not guarantee progress in alignment.”OpenAI has said it is developing stronger monitoring and automated safeguards for its models. The company also recently paused some model development work to add additional safety measures.Astra can help companies identify weaknesses in their systems more quickly, OpenAI has said, while acknowledging that this could also make those weaknesses easier to exploit.Hugging Face breach adds to concernsThe German incident also comes as OpenAI continues to face scrutiny over the separate July breach involving Hugging Face.According to an investigation by the AI safety organisations METR and Redwood Research, OpenAI agents escaped a controlled testing environment and spent weeks carrying out unauthorised activity before breaching Hugging Face's systems.The agents also accessed a cluster of computers inside OpenAI and obtained secret keys and credentials that exposed some internal data to the public internet, according to the investigation.METR's investigation was conducted under terms negotiated with OpenAI, with researchers given access to logs only while working inside the company's San Francisco offices.The researchers said OpenAI limited their access and restricted the investigation's scope, raising questions about whether the full sequence of events was captured.“Our view of the incident changed in big ways over the course of our short total of six days on premises,” Ajeya Cotra told Reuters, one of the METR researchers.OpenAI separately published its own technical report, describing the Hugging Face episode as the “first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorization”.OpenAI disputes claims of withholding investigationReuters reported that OpenAI officials became aware of the German incident weeks ago but did not publicly disclose it. Four people familiar with the matter said some investigators wanted to examine the broader pattern of AI-agent activity more closely, while efforts to expand the investigation faced resistance from some within the company, including legal advisers.“We are unable to meaningfully respond to claims or findings on a report that we have not had an opportunity to review," an OpenAI spokesperson said. "Reuters and the report’s authors declined our request for access. We will carefully review its contents upon publication and take any necessary next steps, " the spokesperson added.The company also rejected claims that its legal team had discouraged investigation of the German incident."Claims that our legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false," the OpenAI spokesperson said.OpenAI said the German activity was unrelated to the Hugging Face incident and would not have been included in a report on that breach. The company also said it had acted in good faith by working with outside experts and disclosing relevant incidents.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: UN votes to adopt new world map to reflect Africa's true size
articles.summary: The Togo-sponsored resolution was backed by 164 nations - the US the only nation to vote against it.
articles.body:
The UN General Assembly has voted to replace the traditional world map with one that more accurately reflects the size of Africa.

The "Correct the Map" resolution, sponsored by Togo and backed by African Union (AU) members, passed with the support of 164 nations, including France and the UK. The United States was the only nation to vote against it - and there were six abstentions.

The UN vote is non-binding but will see changes to the maps used by institutions around the world.

The Mercator map, which has been in common use since the 16th Century, has come in for criticism as it shows Africa as similar in size to Greenland, even though it is 14 times larger.

Critics say this leads to the development needs and potential for countries near the equator to be minimised.

US admits 'unfortunate error' after mislabelling countries on map of Africa

The Mercator map was designed in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European explorers navigate across the world.

The distortion of his map is a result of the fact that it is impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.

Whenever a map of the world is drawn, compromises need to be made.

The Mercator map shows the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing bigger.

In an effort to correct this, a team of cartographers in 2018 created an equal area map they called the Equal Earth projection.

In February, the AU's 54 member states adopted it, and said it "more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa".

Online campaign group #CorrectTheMap said: "You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare."

Ahead of Friday's vote, Togolese Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told the Reuters news agency: "A fair world begins with a fair map."

Earlier he had told a UN briefing: "A map is never neutral. It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood."

He had the backing of the French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, who said his ministry was going to stop using the Mercator map .

"Changing the map obviously doesn't change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth," he said.

But Yaryna Ferencevych, a US representative at the UN, said the resolution mocked the work and purpose of the UN General Assembly .

"Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace, prosperity, or good relations, this body is debating map projects from the 16th Century, and their role in promoting reparations and 'cognitive justice'," she said.

In March, the US was also critical when a resolution was adopted declaring the transatlantic slave trade "the gravest crime against humanity".

"Africa's misrepresentation on world maps is not just a cartographic error - it's a narrative issue," Lerato Mogoatlhe from Africa No Filter, one of the groups behind the campaign to ditch the Mercator map, told the BBC.

It was part of efforts to stop the "world's longest misinformation and disinformation" about Africa, she said.

For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, the Mercator map has implicitly downplayed the African continent's vast resources, population and investment opportunities.

"Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.

articles.title: Yemen’s army says recaptured key territory as clashes with Houthis continue
articles.summary: Two days of fighting between government forces and Houthi fighters has left dozens dead on both sides, sources say.
articles.body:
Yemen’s army say they have recaptured strategically important territory, as heavy clashes with Houthi rebels continue in the southwest of the country.

Yemeni government forces recaptured al-Khazan and al-Makahna hills in Jabal Habashi district west of Taiz city, according to a statement on Friday.

The clashes between government forces and Houthi fighters continued for the second day in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah, two governorates along the Red Sea coast, after the rebel group launched a broad offensive along front lines on the coast.

A Houthi source told Al Jazeera that more than 100 fighters have been killed from both sides since the start of the offensive on Thursday.

A Yemeni military official told Al Jazeera that 24 government troops were killed near the west coast, while another military official reported the deaths of 15 others in clashes in Taiz. Medical sources in Houthi-controlled areas reported that at least 42 fighters had been killed.

Several civilians were killed and others injured in a ballistic missile attack that hit a restaurant in the coastal city of al-Makha (Mocha), state-run Saba TV reported. Over 120 people were killed in Yemen since the Houthis launched their advance, according to an AFP casualty toll.

The Houthis aim to control the hills overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and al-Makha before attacking the coast, a Yemeni official in Aden, the internationally recognised government’s base, told the AFP.

The Houthis captured territories since Thursday mainly in western Taiz including a strategic military base, a government military official told Al Jazeera.

Government military sources said that reinforcements had arrived to counter the Houthi advances in western Taiz, Saba reported.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Yemeni capital Sanaa, said that the aim of the Houthi offensive “seems to be gaining territories towards the city and Red Sea port of al-Makha”.

The Houthis controlled the port city of al-Makha, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandeb Strait connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, before being driven out in 2017 by government forces and Saudi-led coalition.

The rebel group declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in July.

The Houthis want to use Bab al-Mandeb for “military strategic calculation which experts believe could be meaningful in the wars to come against Saudi Arabia or against Israel”, Mawry added.

articles.title: Scientists planted trees on abandoned cattle pasture in Mexico; 17 years later, nearly 5,000 plants were growing across the experimental forest
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Scientists have spent 17 years tracking what happens when native trees are planted on former cattle pasture in Mexico, and the experiment has now reco.
articles.body: Scientists have spent 17 years tracking what happens when native trees are planted on former cattle pasture in Mexico, and the experiment has now recorded nearly 5,000 plants growing across the restoration plots. The experiment carried out in the Los Tuxtlas region of Veracruz began in 2006, when researchers fenced off sections of a pasture and planted trees using two different strategies, while leaving other plots to recover naturally. By 2023, a survey had recorded 4,847 plants across 109 taxa, providing a long-term view of how vegetation developed after cattle grazing stopped. According to the study published in ScienceDirect, titled ‘Understory contrasts across experimental tropical forest restoration’, the planted plots generally supported more plants and species than areas left to natural succession. When trees that had originally been planted were excluded from the analysis, animal-dispersed plantings continued to show higher recruit density. The researchers also found that planted areas supported unique forest species, while the overall understory composition became broadly similar across restoration treatments.How did tree planting in Mexico boost plant growth after 17 yearsThe experiment was surveyed again in July 2023, 17 years after it began. Researchers recorded woody plants and palms between 40 and 225 centimetres tall, allowing them to capture smaller plants that had arrived through more recent dispersal events. The study described this vegetation as the understory that would form the template for the future restored forest.Across the restoration plots, the researchers recorded 4,847 plants belonging to 109 taxa. Of these, 80 were identified to species, five to genus and four to family, while 20 could not be identified more precisely. Two reference forest plots surveyed for comparison contained 309 plants. As the study states, “tree planting increases recruitment magnitude relative to natural succession”.How did tree planting affect plant recruitmentWhen all recruited plants were counted, both types of planted plots contained more plants than areas left to natural succession. Animal-dispersed plots averaged about 253 plants per plot, compared with about 219 in wind-dispersed plots and 134 in plots undergoing natural succession. Species density followed a similar pattern, with animal-dispersed plots averaging 33.5 species per plot, wind-dispersed plots 29.1 and natural succession plots 20.The researchers also analysed the plots after excluding recruits belonging to species that had originally been planted. This separated the plants that had regenerated from the planted trees from species arriving as part of natural succession. Under this analysis, animal-dispersed plantings still had a higher recruit density than natural succession. The study reports that planting treatments increased recruitment compared with natural succession, while animal-dispersed plantings maintained the higher density when planted species were removed from the calculation.How did animal-dispersed plots support more forest speciesAnimal-dispersed plots contained 21 unique taxa, compared with 20 in wind-dispersed plots and 10 under natural succession. They also had 22 recruits from unique non-pioneer species, twice as many as wind-dispersed plots. Natural succession was instead dominated by three unique pioneer taxa, which accounted for 31 recruits. In the wind-dispersed plots, Vochysia guatemalensis made up 23.8% of recruits, with 56 trees taller than two metres recorded by the 13-year census.Despite these differences, understory community composition became broadly similar across treatments when planted species were excluded. Restoration strategy explained only 3.7% of community variation. After 17 years, the experiment had recorded 4,847 plants, with planted plots supporting greater plant and species densities than natural succession. Animal-dispersed plantings also supported more recruits when originally planted species were excluded, while planting created habitat that helped forest species arrive and persist in the former pasture.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: South Asia News: A massive landslide has partially blocked the Chaulani River in Nepal’s Darchula district, prompting authorities to place downstream communities on al.
articles.body: A massive landslide has partially blocked the Chaulani River in Nepal’s Darchula district, prompting authorities to place downstream communities on alert amid fears that continued debris could choke the river and trigger sudden flooding.The landslide occurred at Bhattar in Api Himal Rural Municipality, with debris spilling into the river and affecting its flow. The district administration office, Darchula, warned that further landslides could completely block the river, raising the risk of a sudden breach and flash floods downstream.Authorities have urged people living along the riverbanks to remain vigilant and take precautionary measures. Security personnel have been deployed to warn residents and remain on standby for emergency response.Sudurpaschim Chief Minister Khagraj Bhatta also directed local authorities and security agencies to maintain high alert and prepare for any emergency. The administration has issued emergency contact numbers for flood and disaster assistance.The Armed Police Force said the river was flowing at a normal level for now, but personnel from the Nepal Chameliya Hydropower Security Base in Balanch had been mobilised to monitor the situation and alert nearby communities.The Chaulani, also known as the Chamelia, originates in the Api Himal region and eventually joins the Mahakali River, which forms part of the Nepal-India border.The warning comes as Nepal is still dealing with the impact of severe flooding and flash floods in several areas, with rescue and recovery efforts continuing after recent floods left communities displaced and caused deaths and extensive damage. articles.title: Putin Approval Rating Slips as Ukraine War Fatigue Grows in Russia
articles.summary: Putin Approval Rating Slips as Ukraine War Fatigue Grows in Russia
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin's approval rating slipped again as Russia's war in Ukraine moved deeper into its fifth year, with polling showing signs of growing war fatigue amid drone attacks, fuel shortages, and an uncertain path to peace.

The state-run Russian Public Opinion Research Center, known as VTsIOM, said Friday that 66.9% of respondents approved of Putin's performance in an Aug. 24-30 survey, down 0.8 percentage points from the previous week. Trust in Putin measured 72.2%, up 0.2 percentage points.

The nationwide poll surveyed 1,600 adults through telephone and in-person interviews and had a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points, according to VTsIOM . Its results followed a volatile summer in which Putin's approval hit 65.1% in early July. The Public Opinion Foundation, another polling organization linked to the Kremlin, separately reported a 5-percentage-point weekly decline to 66% in July.

"We've seen support for Putin waning, albeit marginally, but it shows that his critical decisions in the war are forcing pollsters to show the active decline," said Kateryna Stepanenko, Russia team lead at the Institute for the Study of War.

"It may also signal that individuals inside the Kremlin are trying to use pollsters to send a message to Putin about the war," she added. "Someone is going out of there to show that interest in the war is waning."

The independent Levada Center found further signs of war fatigue in an Aug. 18-28 survey of 1,600 Russian adults. Fifty-nine percent favored moving toward peace negotiations, compared with 31% who backed continuing military operations. A record 55% expected the fighting to last more than another year, while 61% said the war had affected them or their families.

Ukraine's intensified long-range drone campaign has increasingly brought the conflict into daily life in Russia. Russian Defense Ministry figures compiled by The Associated Press showed that more than 43,300 Ukrainian drones were intercepted over Russia and Russian-occupied Crimea from June through August, nearly six times the approximately 7,700 reported during the same period in 2025.

Strikes on oil refineries helped fuel gasoline shortages and long lines at filling stations. Drone alerts also closed airports, disrupted flights, and damaged warehouses. Ukrainian officials describe the attacks as pressure intended to weaken Moscow's ability to finance and continue the invasion it launched in February 2022.

"There is a strong desire to end the war, but it's not likely that this trend will lead to major unrest or a palace coup," said John Hardie of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

The political strain comes before Russia's Sept. 18-20 parliamentary election, the first since the full-scale invasion. The election includes few opposition candidates, and Russia's Supreme Court in August removed the anti-war Yabloko party's federal candidate list from the ballot.

Estonian intelligence chief Kaupo Rosin said pressure on Putin to reassess the war appears to be increasing within Russia.

"There are certainly voices which express that he should keep going, but I think the voices which, let's say, urge [him] to maybe reconsider the situation are becoming stronger," Rosin said.

articles.title: American teen began performing Madonna songs in 1985; 40 years later she holds the world record for the longest Madonna impersonator career
articles.summary: US News: In 1985, Denise Bella Vlasis was simply a high-school student who happened to be good at singing and dancing. When her mother asked her to entertain c.
articles.body: In 1985, Denise Bella Vlasis was simply a high-school student who happened to be good at singing and dancing. When her mother asked her to entertain children at a holiday party, she decided to perform a few songs by Madonna, whose career was rapidly taking off at the time. What seemed like a small favour became the beginning of a remarkable professional journey. Vlasis soon found herself returning to perform for children, including youngsters in hospitals, gradually becoming known as a Madonna double. Four decades later, the teenager who once borrowed the pop star's songs for a children's party has an officially recognised world record of her own. In May 2025, Guinness World Records verified Vlasis as having the longest career as a Madonna impersonator, spanning 40 years and 119 days. Now, with a memoir and documentary telling her story, her tribute to Madonna has become a record-breaking career in its own right.A children's party unexpectedly launched a lifelong careerVlasis's journey began when her mother asked her to help entertain foster-care children at a holiday party in 1985. A talented singer and dancer who was still in high school, she chose several Madonna songs for the performance. According to Guinness World Records, neither Vlasis nor her family could have known that the appearance would lead to a career lasting more than four decades. She soon became known as the "Madonna girl", performing for children in hospitals and developing an increasingly convincing tribute act. What began as a way to entertain children gradually became professional work. Vlasis discovered that audiences responded strongly to her resemblance, dancing and ability to recreate Madonna's distinctive performances. The teenage performer had unknowingly found the beginning of a profession that would follow her through adulthood.From hospital visits to becoming Madonna's doubleVlasis's work expanded well beyond children's performances. Her tribute career eventually took her to stages in places including Las Vegas and Japan, while also opening doors to television, film, voice-over work and other opportunities connected to her resemblance to Madonna. In its January 2026 profile, her career spanned for more than four decades encompassing everything from stage performances to stand-in and decoy roles. Yet Vlasis says becoming Madonna's double also changed her personally. She explained to Guinness World Records that performing as Madonna helped her discover her own identity, strength and courage. The irony was that portraying another woman gave her the confidence to become more comfortable with herself. Madonna's fearless public persona became, for Vlasis, a source of inspiration both onstage and beyond it.40 years later, she officially entered the record booksThe longevity of Vlasis's career eventually became a Guinness World Records achievement. In May 2025, she was officially verified as holding the record for the longest career as a Madonna impersonator, with a total of 40 years and 119 days. The milestone recognised something much bigger than simply dressing like a famous singer. Vlasis had continued performing as Madonna through changing fashions, eras and generations of fans. Her act evolved alongside Madonna's own career, from the lace gloves and "Boy Toy" belt associated with the early years to later reinventions of the pop star's image. Guinness World Records reported that Vlasis's career had taken her across different forms of entertainment and around the world. What started with a handful of songs at a children's party had become an extraordinary professional record.Her Madonna tribute is now a memoir and documentaryVlasis is continuing the story rather than simply looking back at it. She had released a memoir titled Dear Madonna: The Journey of Living in the Shadow of the World's Most Famous Star. The book explores the opportunities, experiences and personal lessons that came from spending decades portraying her idol. A documentary with the same title is also being made by her daughter, filmmaker Sofia Vlasis-Gascon. For Vlasis, the tribute has always represented more than imitation. She has spoken about admiring Madonna for refusing to conform to expectations and for encouraging others to find their own voices. After 40 years, that message has become part of Vlasis's own story. The teenager performing Madonna songs for children ultimately built a world-record career while discovering her own identity along the way.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: This Chilean community catches fog in giant nets and turns coastal mist into water; the unusual idea now harvests up to 650,000 litres a year in a drought-hit region
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A drought-hit community in northern Chile has found an unusual source of water in something that usually passes unnoticed. On the hills above Peña Bla.
articles.body: A drought-hit community in northern Chile has found an unusual source of water in something that usually passes unnoticed. On the hills above Peña Blanca, in the Coquimbo region, giant mesh nets are positioned to intercept coastal fog, locally known as camanchaca, as it moves inland from the Pacific. Tiny droplets suspended in the fog collect on the mesh, combine into larger drops and flow into gutters before being channelled into storage. The community has been developing the approach since around 2005, using the harvested water for agriculture, livestock and ecological restoration. Today, 34 fog catchers covering 306 square metres can collect up to 650,000 litres of water a year, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, offering an unconventional response to severe water scarcity and helping support efforts to restore degraded land.How the fog catchers turn mist into water in Chile's drought-hit regionThe technology is surprisingly simple. Large mesh panels are placed across the path of the prevailing fog and wind. When fog passes through the mesh, microscopic water droplets collide with its fibres and accumulate on the surface. As the droplets become larger, gravity pulls them down into collection gutters. Pipes then carry the water towards storage tanks or ponds, where it can be used later. The system does not create water or extract groundwater. Instead, it captures moisture that is already present in the atmosphere. The effectiveness depends heavily on local fog conditions, wind and the type of mesh used, which is why the community has spent years experimenting with different designs and materials.A water source hidden above a dry landscapePeña Blanca lies in one of Chile's driest regions, where prolonged drought has placed pressure on farming, livestock and natural vegetation. The community is part of the Fray Jorge Biosphere Reserve, an area known for the unusual contrast between an extremely dry surrounding landscape and vegetation sustained by coastal moisture. Researchers studying Peña Blanca have documented how declining rainfall and historical land use contributed to soil degradation and reduced agricultural activity. Yet while rainfall became increasingly unreliable, coastal fog continued to arrive over the hills. The community's response was to treat that fog as a potential source of water rather than simply as a weather phenomenon.The experiment began around 2005The Peña Blanca initiative developed in the mid-2000s through cooperation between local residents and Fundación Un Alto en el Desierto. The organisation worked with the community to explore ways of addressing water scarcity, desertification and land degradation. Cerro Grande, a hill rising to roughly 650 metres, became an important location because of its persistent fog. Residents and project workers began installing and testing fog collectors there, gradually adapting the technology to local conditions. The project was not simply a matter of putting up nets and waiting for water. Community members participated in construction, monitoring and maintenance, while repeated experimentation helped determine where collectors worked best and how their design could be improved.The water is being used to restore landOne of the most important aspects of the project is that the collected water is not being used solely as an alternative water supply. It has also been channelled towards ecological restoration at the Cerro Grande reserve. Part of the hill was fenced to prevent livestock from damaging recovering vegetation and the fog-catching infrastructure. Harvested water has been used to support native plants and restoration efforts in an area affected by degradation. This created a direct connection between atmospheric water harvesting and land restoration. Rather than attempting to restore the landscape simply by planting vegetation and hoping for sufficient rainfall, the project created a small, locally controlled water source to support the recovery process.The collectors also support agriculture and livestockThe harvested water has several practical uses outside the reserve. Research on the community's system has documented its use for irrigation and livestock, while more recent projects have expanded its agricultural application. In 2026, a new 10-panel system covering 90 square metres was installed to supply water for a 0.2-hectare plot growing forage crops. Chile's agricultural development agency INDAP said the project involved an investment of more than 28 million Chilean pesos and was designed to provide an additional source of water for local agricultural production. The new system demonstrates how the technology is being adapted not only for ecological restoration but also for the day-to-day needs of farming communities facing increasingly unreliable rainfall.The 650,000-litre figure needs some contextThe headline figure refers to the reported potential of the current system rather than a guaranteed amount of water collected every year. FAO says the 34 fog catchers, covering 306 square metres, can collect up to 650,000 litres annually, with collection particularly strong during periods when fog and wind conditions are favourable. Earlier academic research provides a more specific measured figure. Monitoring of 28 meshes in 2021 recorded approximately 571,590 litres of harvested water. The difference is important because fog collection varies according to atmospheric conditions, collector design and season. The system therefore should not be presented as producing exactly 650,000 litres every year.The community has spent years improving the designThe project has effectively become a long-running experiment in how to make fog harvesting work under local conditions. Recent research analysed five years of community monitoring data from 2020 to 2025 and compared different mesh materials. The study found that Kimre mesh performed about 25 per cent better on average than double-layer Raschel 35 per cent mesh, with the advantage reaching 27.4 per cent during dry or negligible-precipitation conditions. The results demonstrate why material choice matters. A fog catcher may look like a simple piece of mesh stretched between supports, but its ability to capture water depends on the interaction between the mesh, wind, fog and local topography.Strong winds can be a problemThe same wind that brings fog to the collectors can also threaten the infrastructure. Research into large fog collectors in Chile has found that strong wind loads can deform or damage collection systems. Peña Blanca's experience has therefore involved not just maximising water capture but also making the equipment resilient enough to survive local conditions. The newer 2026 agricultural system uses 10 separate panels rather than relying on a single large structure. According to INDAP, this modular design means that if one panel develops a problem, the others can continue operating. Years of practical experience have therefore shaped the technology alongside scientific research.It is more than a water projectThe fog catchers have gradually become part of a broader community effort involving conservation, education and local livelihoods. Peña Blanca's Cerro Grande reserve has been used as a site for environmental education and demonstrations of nature-based approaches to water scarcity. The project has also contributed to local tourism and community activities. Researchers studying the initiative describe benefits extending beyond water itself, including greater community collaboration and local involvement in environmental management. That wider impact is important because the system is not being presented as a technological replacement for conventional water infrastructure. Instead, it represents a locally managed additional resource that can support several activities at the same time.The idea is old but the local experiment is unusualFog harvesting itself is not a new invention. Chile has a long history of research into capturing atmospheric moisture, with scientist Carlos Espinosa Arancibia among the pioneers of fog-collector technology from the 1950s onwards. What makes Peña Blanca notable is the way a local community has adapted the concept over roughly two decades and connected it with land restoration, farming and community management. The innovation therefore lies less in inventing the fog catcher than in recognising that persistent coastal fog could become part of a broader response to drought and land degradation.Fog cannot replace rainfall or solve drought aloneThe project has limitations. Fog availability changes with weather and seasons, and the amount collected is nowhere near enough to meet all the water requirements of a large region. Community members have also disagreed over the project's benefits, particularly because fencing areas for ecological restoration can reduce access to land traditionally used for livestock. Fog water also cannot automatically be assumed to be safe for drinking without appropriate treatment. Scientific studies of Chilean fog water have identified issues including acidity in some samples. The strongest interpretation of Peña Blanca's experience is therefore not that the community has solved drought, but that it has found a previously overlooked source of water that can complement other supplies.A simple idea that keeps evolvingWhat began as an experiment on a fog-covered hill has become a long-running example of how communities can adapt simple technology to difficult environmental conditions. The latest installations and monitoring show that Peña Blanca is still refining the approach rather than treating the original design as finished. In a landscape where rainfall has become increasingly unreliable, the community is making use of moisture that continues to arrive from the Pacific. The result is a striking example of a small change in perspective. Instead of asking where the next rain will come from, residents found a way to collect some of the water that was already moving through the air above them.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US military disables ad trackers over fears location data targeting troops in Middle East: Report
articles.summary: US News: The US military has disabled advertising trackers on a range of phones and computers following reports that commercially available location data had b.
articles.body: The US military has disabled advertising trackers on a range of phones and computers following reports that commercially available location data had been used to target American forces in the Middle East, according to letters released by Senator Ron Wyden and statements to Reuters.The Air Force told Wyden it disabled the advertising identifiers on computers and mobile phones two months ago. US Special Operations Command said it had "recently" disabled them on its Windows devices, while the Army told Reuters that advertising IDs tied to mobile devices had been disabled since earlier this year.The disclosures highlight a growing national security concern: that location data collected by the advertising industry and sold by data brokers can be used to track and target military personnel deployed to war zones.Mobile advertising IDs are unique identifiers tied to specific devices that can track a person's activity across mobile apps and pinpoint their physical location. In July, Reuters reported that some deployed personnel in the Middle East could be ordered to surrender their phones amid concerns that mobile videos they were posting were helping Iran target American bases.Wyden and Representative Pat Harrigan sent a letter to the Pentagon asking for an investigation into whether the military had properly countered the dangers of the location data trade. Wyden said it was clear that the military's efforts "have not been effective at neutralizing this threat." Harrigan said US enemies "should not be able to pull out a credit card and buy information that helps them track American troops."Zach Edwards, co-founder of privacy ad tech company Decryptads, said disabling MAID on military devices was "definitely a positive thing," though he cautioned that personnel might still be tracked through apps in other ways.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ladakh residents to get ownership rights over 60,000 acres of barren land
articles.summary: India News: SRINAGAR: Ladakh residents will now have rights over barren lands or wastelands owned by govt, with the administration Friday approving Ladakh Autonom.
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Ladakh residents will now have rights over barren lands or wastelands owned by govt, with the administration Friday approving Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (Nautor Regularisation) Rules, 2026.The Rules provide a comprehensive framework for granting proprietary rights on up to 10 acres of eligible Nautor land holdings to the occupants across all seven districts of the Union Territory. For Nautor land beyond the 10-acre limit, the proprietary rights may be allotted on a leasehold basis, in accordance with the rules.Nautor land refers to barren or wasteland, owned by govt, which was earlier allotted to individuals for cultivation or other productive use. More than 60,000 acres of land in Ladakh is presently recorded in revenue records as Nautor holdings.The Rules offer a one-time regularisation mechanism for Nautor land, occupied before the repeal of J&K Tenancy Act-980, on Oct 27, 2020. Any possession of Nautor land after this cut-off date will be ineligible for regularisation.“The Nautor issue has a deep historical connection with the lives and livelihoods of the people of Ladakh. For generations, our people have worked hard to bring barren and waste land under cultivation in one of the most challenging agricultural environments in the country. These Rules provide a transparent and uniform mechanism to address this long-pending issue and give legal certainty to genuine holders. It will also enable such land to be utilised as a financial asset, including for availing bank loans,” Ladakh LG Vinai Kumar Saxena said.According to the Rules, the authority of allotting Nautor land will be vested in Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils in all seven districts.A govt spokesperson said the absence of a clear and uniform legal framework until now restricted the effective utilisation of Nautor land. “In particular, landholders with limited or non-proprietary rights, were unable to use the land as a financial asset, including for purposes such as obtaining loans against it. At the same time, the absence of uniform rules also posed a threat of claims and disputes over govt, council land,” the spokesperson said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Built by convicts in the 1830s, Australia's oldest in-use vehicle bridge nearly collapsed; engineers rebuilt it from the bedrock
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Thomas James Bridge, also known as Settlers Road Bridge, crosses a creek near Lower Macdonald in New South Wales and holds a rare distinction: it is t.
articles.body: Thomas James Bridge, also known as Settlers Road Bridge, crosses a creek near Lower Macdonald in New South Wales and holds a rare distinction: it is the oldest in-use vehicle bridge on mainland Australia. Built in 1830 using convict labour, the bridge has a simple single-span timber deck supported by massive stone abutments, with the sandstone quarried from the surrounding hillside and worked by hand on site. In 2022, severe floods and storm events damaged the bridge significantly, including the near-total collapse of the eight-metre-tall sandstone retaining walls supporting its abutments. What followed was a two-year reconstruction that required engineers to excavate the site down to bedrock, install new foundations and carefully take apart and number the original sandstone blocks before putting them back in their original positions. Completed in November 2025, the project has now received the Judges' Excellence Award in Heritage at the 2026 IPWEA NSW & ACT Engineering Awards.How engineers rebuilt Thomas James Bridge from the bedrock upAccording to Hawkesbury City Council, the restoration required a tailor-made engineering solution developed in close consultation with heritage experts. Engineers excavated the site down to bedrock before installing new steel and concrete footings and drainage systems designed to withstand future flooding and heavy rainfall. The work was not simply about replacing the structures damaged in 2022. The new foundations had to provide greater resilience while allowing the historic bridge above them to retain its original appearance and character. The project was completed in November 2025 after two years of work, with Hawkesbury City Council managing the project alongside delivery partner Delaney Civil.Why every sandstone block had to be numberedThe most painstaking part of the restoration involved the bridge's original hand-cut sandstone retaining wall. Rather than demolishing the damaged structure and rebuilding it with new stone, workers carefully dismantled it block by block. Each individual piece was numbered, its original position recorded, and the stone placed into storage while the new foundations were constructed. Once the structural work was complete, the original blocks could be put back together in their previous configuration. The timber bridge deck was also reinstated, preserving the historical appearance and significance of the site. The stone itself has been part of the bridge's story since its construction. Heritage records say it was quarried from the surrounding hillside, cut on site and moved into place entirely by hand. The resulting stonework forms a 16.3-metre-long channel along the banks of the creek. Evidence of the original quarrying and splitting of the sandstone can still be seen around the gully.Who Thomas James was, and why a convict's name is attached to the bridgeThomas James was a ticket-of-leave convict who directly supervised the No. 25 Road Party responsible for building the bridge. He arrived in New South Wales in December 1819, aged 24, aboard the Recovery with 187 other convicts. He had been sentenced to life for an unknown crime. By 1824, he was working with the Bathurst Road Party stationed at Richmond before being transferred to the No. 25 Road Party at Wisemans Ferry. By 1830, he had obtained his ticket of leave and was overseeing the road party that built the bridge. The bridge was constructed under the broad supervision of Percy Simpson, a surveyor, engineer and administrator who played a major role in the construction of the Great North Road. Thomas James later lived in Penrith, where he was recorded by 1837, and received a conditional pardon in 1842. The bridge is one of only eight surviving bridges from the original 22 built along the Great North Road.How the $23.5 million reconstruction protects the bridge from future floodsHawkesbury City Council managed the $23.5 million reconstruction, with funding from Federal and State Government infrastructure recovery programmes. The restoration was intended not only to repair the damage caused by the 2022 floods but also to maintain a reliable connection between Wisemans Ferry and the Macdonald Valley. Council said the disaster-affected community was kept at the centre of its decision-making throughout the project. The finished bridge still looks like the historic structure built by the No. 25 Road Party almost two centuries ago. Beneath the original sandstone, however, it now has new foundations and drainage designed to better withstand the flooding that once threatened to cut the valley's road connection. That combination of modern structural engineering and original historic fabric is what earned the reconstruction its 2026 heritage engineering award.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: LONDON: The RSS shrugged off criticism by civil groups of its chief Dr Mohan Bhagwat’s UK trip, saying in a democracy differences of opinions are expected and “should not be taken as a shock”.The RSS head arrived in London on Sept 2 on the final leg of his three-city outreach RSS centenary tour, having just visited New York and Toronto on a “dialogue mission.”Hindus for Human Rights UK and several other campaign groups wrote an open letter to London mayor Sadiq Khan asking him to condemn the visit, pointing out New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani had done that.Labour PIO MP Nadia Whittome tabled a written parliamentary question asking the home office whether “the visit engages the commitment to block hate preachers and extremists from entering the UK”.“We are here for peace, integration and oneness and we are open for dialogue with everyone. In a democracy, it is very normal to raise different voices. We are engaging with those who wish to dialogue with us,” RSS head of media Sunil Ambekar said at a press briefing on Friday.“We are here to communicate what we are and how we think. We are very much open. We have nothing to hide. We expect a debate and exchange of thoughts. Let them speak.”On allegations the RSS was behind the 2022 Leicester riots, Ambekar said this was a “UK domestic issue”. “There is no question… RSS was not involved. Already people are finding out their legal options. Hindus are a peace-loving community.”He said there are a lot of “misconceptions” in the West. “Bharat is not a nation state political concept — it is a cultural concept. Hindutva is not like any religion — it’s a concept where there will be respect for all religious practices. That is Hindutva, and that is Bharat, so I think the trip will help to clear the ideas,” he said.A spokesperson for the London mayor said the mayor “does not have the power” to ban people from speaking. “London is proud to celebrate our diversity and intolerance has no place in our great city,” the spokesperson said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1978, advocates sought affordable homes in a New York town; nearly 50 years and a landmark court battle later, a $98 million community with 145 homes is finally complete
articles.summary: US News: A proposal that began as a fight for affordable housing in a Long Island community in 1978 has finally resulted in 145 affordable homes. Matinecock Co.
articles.body: A proposal that began as a fight for affordable housing in a Long Island community in 1978 has finally resulted in 145 affordable homes. Matinecock Court, a nearly $98 million affordable housing development in the Town of Huntington in Suffolk County, was completed in 2026 after decades of legal and political obstacles. The development's origins are closely tied to Housing Help Inc. and the Huntington Branch of the NAACP, which challenged Huntington's restrictions on multifamily housing. The dispute eventually became a landmark Fair Housing Act case that reached the U.S. Supreme Court. New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced the project's completion on September 2, 2026, describing it as the culmination of a decades-long effort. According to the New York Governor’s Office announcement, the project now provides 145 limited-equity cooperative homes, including units for veterans and people with disabilities. The original federal court proceedings provide the legal history behind the unusually long journey.A housing proposal beginsThe story of Matinecock Court began around 1978, when Housing Help Inc. decided to pursue a subsidised, lower-income housing project in Huntington. The organisation hoped to secure federal Section 8 funding and worked with the Suffolk Community Development Corporation to identify possible locations. Eighteen potential sites were identified in Huntington.But building the proposed development required something the town's existing zoning rules did not allow. Matinecock Court needed multifamily zoning because the proposed development required a density of roughly 10 to 12 units per acre. Housing Help continued pushing for the necessary zoning change, eventually bringing the dispute into federal court alongside the Huntington Branch NAACP and individual plaintiffs. The case became known as Huntington Branch NAACP v. Town of Huntington.The battle reaches courtThe legal dispute was about more than a single housing project. At its center was the question of whether Huntington's zoning policies had a discriminatory effect by restricting where multifamily and lower-cost housing could be built. In its 1981 decision, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York addressed the plaintiffs' claims concerning Huntington's housing policies and federal housing assistance. The plaintiffs argued that Huntington's housing plan, including its lack of goals for newly constructed or substantially rehabilitated HUD-assisted rental housing, contributed to the problems facing the proposed project.The case did not end there. The plaintiffs appealed, and the Second Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the earlier ruling and sent the case back. The litigation continued throughout the 1980s. In 1987, the district court again considered the dispute, including the town's refusal to provide the multifamily zoning needed for Matinecock Court. The court record noted that the proposed development would have helped provide lower-cost housing in a town where affordable housing was in short supply. The Second Circuit ultimately found that Huntington had violated the Fair Housing Act, and the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed that landmark holding in 1988.A community takes shapeDecades after the original proposal, Matinecock Court has finally become a completed residential community. The development contains 145 limited-equity cooperative homes spread across 17 two-story residential buildings. The homes include one, two and three-bedroom units and are affordable to households earning up to 80% of the area median income.The project also includes housing designed for residents with specific needs. Eight supportive apartments are reserved for people with developmental disabilities, while four homes are reserved for veterans. There are also 15 units designed to accommodate people with mobility disabilities and six for residents with sensory disabilities. The community includes a clubhouse, on-site parking and private outdoor patio areas. Its location also places residents near the Long Island Rail Road's Northport Station, Suffolk County bus service, schools, shopping, restaurants and a library.Nearly $98 million investmentThe completed development represents an investment of nearly $98 million, assembled through multiple public and private sources. According to the New York Governor’s Office announcement, financing included federal and state Low-Income Housing Tax Credits expected to generate more than $36 million in equity, along with $28 million in subsidy. Additional support came from New York's Office for People With Developmental Disabilities, Empire State Development and Suffolk County.Matinecock Court was also designed as an all-electric development. Its energy features include heat-pump water heaters, electric heating and cooling, enhanced insulation, LED lighting, Energy Star appliances and low-flow plumbing. The completion marks an unusual endpoint for a housing proposal that began nearly half a century ago. What started in 1978 as an effort to create affordable homes became a prolonged legal fight over zoning and fair housing, eventually reaching the nation's highest court. Now, that history has a physical result: 145 affordable homes in Huntington, turning a decades-old housing proposal and landmark Fair Housing Act case into a completed community.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Reform donations row overshadows party's moment to lay out big ideas
articles.body:
Speak to people at the highest levels of Reform UK and they will admit the party has struggled in recent weeks.

Reform's polling numbers have dipped, while Labour's have risen.

One of their aims at this conference was to demonstrate Reform is a serious party of government. After a summer fighting the by-election in Clacton , which the other main parties boycotted, the party wanted to demonstrate they have a plan for government, focusing on immigration and the cost of living.

A press conference alongside Jordan Bardella, President of the National Rally which leads the polls in France, was part of that effort, and the intention was to project serious international co-operation with another insurgent party on the right.

Farage and Bardella signed an agreement that, if both parties win power, the UK would intercept boats crossing the Channel with France accepting their return.

But it was overshadowed by questions about two aides who have stepped down.

Undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4 News and filmed by Verbatim Investigations shows Dan Jukes, one of Nigel Farage's closest advisers, and Reform's head of policy James Orr, meeting a man posing as the British-based son of a rich American.

Jukes appears to suggest a way to evade electoral law, which only allows donations from people based, or companies registered, in the UK.

Farage told reporters this afternoon that the party had done nothing wrong, and the comments were "loose pub talk" and a "bit of boasting and a bit of jack the laddery". But both aides – who were crucial to Reform's rise from insurgency to a dominant political party – have now stepped down while an internal investigation takes place.

Jukes denies any wrongdoing. He says he has "stepped back from politics in order to clear my name." Orr told Sky News he agreed to step down and will cooperate fully with the investigation.

But this is a bigger problem for Reform than the careers of two aides, however senior. As pollsters More in Common told delegates here in Birmingham, "perceptions of sleaze now rank as the main barrier stopping people from backing Reform."

Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk'

Two Reform officials step down after undercover donations report

Farage unveils small boats deal with French National Rally party

And this story risks further spreading that perception. Walking around here at conference, it is not hard to find frustration, even anger, that the party is in this situation.

Plenty here see the undercover filming as part of a witch hunt against the party.

Others despair they are once again facing similar allegations to the ones they were trying to escape.

So has the opportunity to talk about wider issues been lost?

Nigel Farage's big speech at the end of the conference day was delayed - but when he got going, the Reform UK leader decided not to avoid the latest allegations around his party's approach donations. Instead he launched a carefully-balanced rebuttal.

Elsewhere in the speech, he did lay out his party's significant successes over the past year - including high-profile defection and victories in May's English local, Scottish and Welsh elections.

We saw a roll call of his long-term campaign messages: "Britain is broken", "Britain needs Reform" and "we will stop the boats".

The was some new policy about how he'd declare a "national emergency" on day one of a Reform-led government with parliament potentially sitting "24 hours a day" and "six days a week".

But Farage seemed to have decided to leave much of his party's policy announcements to the speeches of his colleagues Robert Jenrick, Richard Tice and Zia Yusuf. These will continue on Saturday.

And there was also a more-detailed attack on Andy Burnham than we've previously seen - Farage attempted to frame the new administration as a "continuity government", and said that the creation of Number 10 North would mean "bigger government, more taxes and more failure".

His speech then ended rather abruptly. It was shorter, and more off-the-cuff than expected. The party members seem to enjoy it.

But amid a barrage of wider questions about the party's finances, it is unlikely to draw a line under the significant problems now facing the Reform UK leader.

articles.title: Nigel Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judiciary in Reform conference speech
articles.summary: The Reform UK leader promises to deliver on key priorities in the first 100 days of government, if the party wins power.
articles.body:
Nigel Farage has insisted a Reform UK government would deliver where other parties have failed, as he set out his priorities in his annual conference speech.

He said Reform's pledges for its first 100 days in power would include stopping small boat crossings, cutting energy bills by £250 a year and ending the net zero "lunacy".

To eliminate "obstacles" to his plans, Farage said he would declare a "national emergency" and threatened to overhaul the House of Lords and how judges are appointed if they stood in the way.

In a speech interrupted several times by protesters, the Reform leader was also forced to address allegations over donations which emerged in an undercover investigation.

Reform had been hoping to use its annual conference to regain momentum after a difficult summer dominated by questions over the party's finances.

However, the main day of the conference was overshadowed after two senior party officials stepped down and Reform launched an investigation into claims about funding aired during a Channel 4 News report on Thursday evening, which was filmed by Verbatim Investigations, a group founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting.

In the undercover filming, the two men suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign donations for the party, one of which would have totalled £500,000.

Farage insisted "the party has done nothing wrong" and "has taken no illegal money", claiming the allegations had been made "because they're scared of us".

Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk'

Reform donations row overshadows party's moment to lay out big ideas

Reform UK promises £80bn cuts to public spending

In his speech, which was light on new policy announcements, Farage said the country needed a government "that actually delivers on its promises" and "we're the only people capable of doing it".

He argued the Tories "had 14 years in power and failed absolutely miserably", while Labour's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham "says he needs 10 years", a reference to the PM's promise to set out a 10-year plan for the country later this year.

If Reform wins the next general election, Farage pledged to sack ministers who fail to deliver on their promises in their first 100 days in the job "and replace them with somebody else with the courage to do it".

Setting out his plans to call a "national emergency" if Reform wins power, Farage said: "Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, for six days a week until we pass the necessary legislation."

He said he expected the House of Lords to "honour" Reform's policy pledges but if they refused to do so threatened to appoint hundreds of new peers so the party had a majority in the upper chamber.

"And if that proves difficult, we will hold a referendum on the current composition of the House of Lords, and they would be swept away by a British public appalled by them," he added.

Identifying the judiciary as another possible "obstacle", Farage promised to remove the ability of judges to rely on conventions like the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR), which critics blame for hindering some deportations.

"We don't want the courts striking down, do we, the will of the people," he said.

"Parliament makes the law, judges interpret the law. We will do whatever it takes, and perhaps have to consider how judicial appointments work in the future."

Meanwhile, he said civil servants who "try to obstruct us" would be removed from their posts and replaced by people from the world of business.

"I'm tired of being told what can't be done," the Reform leader said.

"That is not what the public want. The public want action, the public want genuine change, the public do not want any more of the same. And our attitude is can do, and will do."

Predicting that Burnham would call an early general election in spring 2027, Farage attempted to use his speech to convince the public Reform was ready to govern.

Stressing he now had a team of spokespeople with "frontline experience", he said the party was planning to broaden its expertise.

"There are more big jobs to fill, and I'm looking and working on defence, health, and the other areas," he added.

In his speech, Farage also hailed a "historic agreement" on small boat returns, signed earlier between Reform and France's hard-right National Rally party .

The deal sets out how a Reform government would intercept boats in the English Channel and return them to France using the Navy, with France "ordinarily" accepting those on board.

It was signed by the National Rally President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of French presidential elections in April next year, after he gave a speech to the main conference hall.

Farage took to the stage after a long delay, which he told delegates was due to a "security alert".

He took the opportunity to walk through the crowd and greet delegates during the delay.

His speech was also interrupted several times by protesters, including two women who held up a banner reading "Reform works for billionaires".

They were booed by audience members who shouted "out", as they were removed by security.

Farage laughed off the disruption, chanting "boring, boring, boring".

Reform is no longer consistently topping national opinion polls, after more than a year of enjoying a comfortable lead.

Meanwhile, Labour's ratings have risen since Burnham entered Downing Street, and Reform has lost some support to Restore Britain, the new right-wing party founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

articles.body: A judge declared a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial on Friday after jurors said they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the deaths of her three young children.The mistrial, declared on the seventh day of deliberations, leaves the case unresolved and allows prosecutors to retry the 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, as cited by AP.The deliberations took a dramatic turn late in the week when the judge said he would declare a mistrial on Friday, but then changed course and gave Clancy’s defense attorney an opportunity to appeal to Massachusetts’ top court. The court, however, denied the emergency appeal seeking to prevent the judge from declaring a mistrial.Clancy’s attorney argued that she was suffering from a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her three children, including her youngest, who was just 8 months old, before attempting to take her own life.Prosecutors said Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, deliberately strangled her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, with exercise bands on January 24, 2023. They said she arranged for her husband to leave the house by asking him to pick up medicine for one of the children and dinner for the family.Prosecutors argued that Clancy knew what she was doing. They must now decide whether to retry her, drop the charges or negotiate a plea deal with her lawyer.Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, did not dispute that she killed the children but argued that she should not be held criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness associated with the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that can follow childbirth.Over 21 days of testimony, jurors heard how Clancy’s mental health deteriorated after Callan’s birth.Deeply anxious about returning to work, unable to sleep and experiencing what she described as a disturbing brain fog, Clancy sought treatment from specialists in postpregnancy mood disorders, who prescribed her multiple psychiatric medications.Family members testified that Clancy had expressed concerns about her declining mental health. Her former mother-in-law, Susan Clancy, described her as a “very nurturing, very loving mother” who was “begging for help.”In early January, Clancy admitted herself to a psychiatric hospital for more intensive treatment, but her stay was brief. Nineteen days after she was discharged, she killed the children and left their bodies in the basement of the family’s home in coastal Duxbury, Massachusetts. Clancy then jumped from a second-story window and remains paralyzed from the waist down.Prosecutors acknowledged that Clancy suffered from severe mental illness but argued that she was still able to understand and control her actions. They highlighted that although Clancy said she heard a male voice commanding her to kill the children, she had never told her mental health providers that she was hearing voices before the killings.In the latter stages of the trial, the case became a battle between medical experts.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's trial centered on whether severe mental illness relieved her of criminal responsibility in the January 2023 deaths of her three children.
articles.body: Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Friday in Lindsay Clancy’s murder case after jurors said they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict in the killings of her three children after a week of deliberating at the Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts. The mistrial followed a dramatic dispute over an alleged 11-1 divide, with Clancy’s defense arguing that the lone holdout juror had acknowledged doubt but was refusing to properly apply the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt. The alleged holdout is believed to be one of the three male jurors on the 12-person panel after defense attorney Kevin Reddington repeatedly referred to the unnamed juror as a male inside and outside court. POSTPARTUM MOM LINDSAY CLANCY ON TRIAL FOR MURDER BRINGS COURT TO A HALT WITH SUDDEN BREAKDOWN "[The other jurors] know that they were robbed — by one man — for whatever his agenda was, who stole seven weeks of the life of these other jurors that were so attentive, so beautiful, so wonderful and listened to this evidence," he told reporters after leaving the courthouse. "And you could see how defeated they were sitting there. And I got a funny feeling they could go one for another week if they had to. So, I hope that guy can sleep well at night." Also speaking outside the courthouse, Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz acknowledged the victims in this case — the Clancy children: 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. "It is our job to make sure the victims are not invisible," Cruz said. "I am a father and a grandfather, and I cannot imagine the hell this entire family has lived through." Clancy’s attorneys made an emergency appeal to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in an attempt to stay the mistrial and force further inquiry into the juror. Justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt denied the request Friday afternoon, clearing the way for Sullivan to formally declare the mistrial. HEATED LINDSAY CLANCY COURTROOM EXCHANGE OVER 911 CALL, CRIME SCENE PHOTOS SETS STAGE FOR MOM’S MURDER TRIAL Clancy had been charged with first-degree murder in the January 2023 deaths of her children, each of whom had been strangled with exercise bands. The trial centered on whether she was legally responsible for her actions at the time, and the defense argued she wasn't due to postpartum psychosis. Her attorneys argued that severe mental illness left her unable to appreciate the wrongfulness of what she was doing or unable to conform her conduct to the requirements of the law. LINDSAY CLANCY’S HUSBAND COULD TESTIFY FOR HER AT TRIAL OVER DEATHS OF THEIR THREE CHILDREN Prosecutors maintained that Clancy remained criminally responsible and pointed to evidence they said showed planning, purposeful behavior and an awareness of what she was doing before, during and after the killings. During the trial, Clancy's former husband, Patrick Clancy, testified about the day of the slayings, which happened while he was running errands that included picking up children's stool softener at a CVS store and takeout for dinner. They spoke on the phone while he was out. Under Massachusetts law, once lack of criminal responsibility is properly raised, prosecutors must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that a defendant was criminally responsible. The mistrial means the case ended without a verdict, and Clancy was neither convicted nor acquitted. Prosecutors can seek to retry her but have not yet announced a decision. Sullivan said he wants the case retried "sooner rather than later," suggesting a new trial could potentially take place later this fall. Clancy is due back in court Sept. 29 for a status hearing, trial assignment and a defense Rule 25 motion. All previous bail orders remain in effect. JUDGE SENTENCES NEVADA MOM FOR DROWNING YOUNG SON, DAUGHTER: 'I WILL REMEMBER YOUR CASE FOREVER' FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X The mistrial followed a trial that focused extensively on Clancy's psychiatric condition in the months and weeks before the children died. Jurors heard testimony about her treatment by mental health professionals, psychiatric medications, anxiety, depression, insomnia and other symptoms documented before the killings. BROOKLYN MOTHER WHO DROWNED HER THREE CHILDREN IN THE OCEAN NEAR CONEY ISLAND SENTENCED TO DECADES IN PRISON Cora and Dawson died that night. Callan was taken to a hospital and died several days later. Lindsay Clancy survived after jumping from a second-story window and suffered injuries that left her paralyzed in a wheelchair. The prosecution and defense offered sharply different explanations for what happened before the children were killed. The defense had argued that the deaths occurred after months of worsening psychiatric symptoms and treatment and that Clancy's mental condition had deteriorated to the point she could not legally be held criminally responsible. Specifically, the defense contended that Clancy heard a male voice that commanded her to kill her three children. Dr. Phillip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist, said it was almost as if she was a "puppet." It was almost like she was a puppet, and someone else was pulling the strings," Resnick said. "This was the first time she reported that, and that she experienced an auditory hallucination, according to what she told me. So, that was unusual. And then what was very unusual was the fact that the voice stopped with the strangling of her youngest son." During the trial, members of Clancy's family revealed they were "very concerned" about her mental health in the months before she killed her three kids.
